narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 52.4% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is just over 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile of your class is substantially lower than the average ranking of about 5.8 among students who were accepted. Your first-year ranking, also in the bottom decile compared with an average around 6.0 among accepted students, added further weight in the same direction.

Your LSAT score of 39 worked in your favor and pulled the prediction toward passing. This score sits slightly above the 37.2 average of accepted applicants, giving the model some reassurance about your potential. However, the two weak class rankings outweighed this positive signal.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.4, middle-income background, and plan to attend full-time were considered but had less impact on the final outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic performance and class standing in law school if you retake courses or enroll elsewhere. You could also consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score further or explore schools with different admissions thresholds. Reapplying with a stronger record of consistent high performance will help the model see you as more likely to pass the bar. (248 words)
